# --- Buttons of the controllers: the finger on a control (touch) ---
group.buttons_of_the_controllers_the_finger_on_a_control_touch = Buttons of the controllers: the finger on a control (touch)
group.buttons_of_the_controllers_the_finger_on_a_control_touch.help = Actions fired when your finger just touches a control, without pressing it (Touch and Index controllers; PS VR2 on SteamVR too). F4 only, in the world; nothing is bound by default.
@remap.right_trigger_touch.label = Right trigger (touch)
@remap.right_trigger_touch.tip_tail = TOUCH, not a press: this fires once when your finger ARRIVES on the control (the capacitive touch of a Touch controller - PS VR2 on SteamVR is one - or an Index controller), nothing more while it stays, and once again the next time it arrives - a game key such as Show items (Alt) is held while the finger stays and let go with it. It is on top of what pressing the same control does (the touch comes first). A Vive, WMR or simple controller reports no touch: nothing happens there. First person (F4), in the world only - not in a menu or with a panel of the mod's own up. Nothing is bound by default; to put the game's run / walk switch here pick "Run / walk switch". The log (d2r-vr-vrcam.log) says which touch inputs your controller reports.
@remap.right_a_touch.label = Right A (touch)
@remap.right_b_touch.label = Right B (touch)
@remap.right_stick_touch.label = Right stick (touch)
@remap.left_trigger_touch.label = Left trigger (touch)
@remap.left_x_touch.label = Left X (touch)
@remap.left_y_touch.label = Left Y (touch)
@remap.left_stick_touch.label = Left stick (touch)

# ===== Tab: Stereo =====
tab.stereo = Stereo

# --- Native OpenXR (the game itself in the headset) ---
group.native_openxr_the_game_itself_in_the_headset = Native OpenXR (the game itself in the headset)
group.native_openxr_the_game_itself_in_the_headset.help = Everything for native OpenXR: brightness, the flat picture for menus, F1 and F3 in real 3D, room-scale walking, Controls without BodyWalk, the skill panel, the eyes' angles and distance, the square window and vibration. Most of it changes live.
openxr.brightness.label = Brightness in the headset
openxr.brightness.tip = Everything the game shows in the headset, darker or brighter: the picture, the flat picture, the toolbar and the map. 1 = as the game draws it. The headset's runtime does it (SteamVR, Virtual Desktop...); one without it leaves the picture as it is - vrcam's log says which.
openxr.flat_distance_m.label = Flat picture: distance, m
openxr.flat_distance_m.tip = Menus and loading (F1 and F3 too, when "F1 and F3 in real 3D" is off) stand this far ahead, where you looked when they came up. F1 in 3D is a window this far away. Farther = smaller in view. An open panel (inventory, trade...) has its own distance, below.
openxr.flat_width_m.label = Flat picture: width, m
openxr.flat_width_m.tip = How wide that picture is - and F1's window in 3D; its height follows the game window's shape.
openxr.views_3d.label = F1 and F3 in real 3D (native OpenXR)
openxr.views_3d.tip = Native OpenXR: F3 (the game on your floor) is the diorama standing in your room, seen with the headset's own eyes - walk round it, lean over it, crouch; it lies on the headset's own floor when it has one (else your height decides), and the world is small there, so the eyes' parallax follows. F1 (from above) is the game's view from above in true perspective seen through a window as wide and as far as the flat picture (below), your hero on its middle: lean left or right to look round things; F1 is in true perspective then, whatever "Real geometry" (UI: F1 above) says. F2 and F4 are in 3D as ever. Menus, loading and the character screens stay the flat picture. Where it is put ("Put the game in front of me", F11, the headset's own recentre) and the size of the diorama are in the F3 group on the Camera tab. Off: F1 and F3 as the flat picture, as before. Switches while the game runs.
openxr.pointer_3d.label = Show the game's mouse pointer in F1 and F3
openxr.pointer_3d.tip = In F1 and F3 in 3D the game is played with the mouse, and the pointer it shows (the gauntlet, the sword over a monster...) used to be nowhere in the headset - the scene stands in the room, there is no picture to show it on. With this on the same pointer is hung on the game's ground where the game's mouse points: the ground point a click would walk to, a few centimetres large, turned to your eyes, its tip on the point. Only a picture: the mouse, the clicks and the hero's movement are not touched. It is shown while the game shows its pointer (it hides it in the controller layout) and the mouse is over the game's window. Off: no pointer in these views, as before. Switches while the game runs.
screen.menu_distance_m.label = Flat picture with a panel open (inventory, trade...): distance, m
screen.menu_distance_m.tip = While the inventory, a trader, the stash or another panel is open in a game, the flat picture moves this far away - smoothly - and back when it closes. With a square window the game's interface is as wide as the picture: farther, its left and right edges come into view. 0 = the distance above. The same setting as "Screen distance while a panel is open" for FlatVR (UI: F4 body).
openxr.busy_guard.label = Never hang on a busy headset (native OpenXR)
openxr.busy_guard.tip = A runtime waits for a headset another app holds for good: FlatVR through BodyWalk Lite, then back to Native, and the game stood until Task Manager. On: the runtime's two blocking calls (the frame wait and the session's start) run on a thread of their own, and the game waits for them a fraction of a second; if they have not come the headset gets no picture that frame and the game goes on flat (the log says so, and when the headset answers). And no headset session is started over a FlatVR that holds the headset and cannot be stopped (BodyWalk Lite has no Game Link): the Status column says to close BodyWalk and restart SteamVR, and it is tried again while FlatVR runs. Needs a game restart. Off: as before. (d2r_vr.ini: wait_frame_ms.)
openxr.reap_drain_max_ms.label = Old swapchains: longest wait to free them, ms (native OpenXR)
openxr.reap_drain_max_ms.tip = A swapchain of ours made again (a new mouse pointer, a menu panel of another size) is freed later, once the graphics card has finished the game's work: waited for 20 ms, doubled each time that was not enough, up to this. With a busy card (the headset's recommended size) 20 ms was never enough, the old ones piled up and SteamVR refused new ones (XR_ERROR_LIMIT_REACHED): the inventory opened with no panel, the pointer gone, a black picture. 20 = as before. Live.
openxr.menus_wait_tracking.label = Menus placed only when the headset is tracked
openxr.menus_wait_tracking.tip = The flat picture (menus, loading, the title screen) and a menu's panel are put in the room only once the headset says your head is tracked - before that a runtime may give a guessed place, and the picture stayed at the floor or behind you. Until then the picture follows your gaze (a headset that never says it is tracked gets 3 seconds). And when the headset's focus comes back after 2 seconds or more away (taken off, the runtime's own menu) they come up in front of you again - for a player who sat down or stood up meanwhile. Live. Off: the first half second follows the gaze, then placed, as before.
openxr.lean_m.label = Head off the body, m
openxr.lean_m.tip = First and third person: how far the head may lean away from the hero's body. Farther, the body follows - walking in the room never takes the camera out of the hero. 0 = turning only.
openxr.roomscale_walk.label = Room-scale walking: your steps in the room walk the hero (F4)
openxr.roomscale_walk.tip = Native OpenXR, VR first person (F4) only. Walk in your room and the hero walks the same way: the plugin gives the game's own walking stick - the one the controller's left stick uses - the direction and the speed of your steps, so the game's pathing, walls, walk / run and speed stay the game's; the hero is never moved or put anywhere by the plugin. The view stays with your head the whole time and the hero catches up under it. Turning your head, nodding or a small lean (the dead zone below) walks nothing. The stick asks the game for your own walking speed (its walk speed follows the stick's tilt; the hero's speed at a full stick is learned as you play), so a steady walk is one steady tilt and the hero walks with you. But the game never walks him slower than a quarter of his full walk (with "walk straight", [input] direct_walk, on by default; without it the gamepad's dead zone makes it about a third) - often faster than a step in a room: then he walks in short pulses at that least walk, stopping where he catches you up (or as far past you as he started behind, while you walk on), so he stays within the dead zone of you; the view is your head's the whole time. A brisk stride can reach a run when the game's Run / Run Lock is on. Turning is never done by it: the hero's facing stays as it is. The controller's left stick wins while it is pushed (the view goes with the hero then, as always). When the hero is blocked (a wall, a monster) and you walk on, the view leaves him by at most the limit below; past it the room slides with you, as "Head off the body" does. A panel or the chat open: no walk, your place is kept. F11 or the headset's own recentre puts the hero under your head again. Off: walking in the room does not move the hero (the body follows the head past "Head off the body", as before). FlatVR: nothing - its camera has no head place to walk by. The log says "room walk - live / holds / stands down" and why. Live.
openxr.roomscale_dead_zone_m.label = Room-scale walking: dead zone, m
openxr.roomscale_dead_zone_m.tip = How far the top of your neck may move off the hero's place before he walks: leaning and swaying inside it walk nothing. Smaller: he follows every small step (and a lean); larger: only real steps walk him. 0: no dead zone of your own - he starts as soon as he can be placed: the game never walks him slower than a quarter of his full walk, so the least he can be moved is about half of what that walks in two of its ticks (a few centimetres; it is learned as you walk). Live.
openxr.roomscale_body.label = Room-scale walking: your body stays under you (smooth)
openxr.roomscale_body.tip = The game never walks the hero slower than a quarter of his full walk, so under that he catches up with your steps in short pulses - the view stays with your head, but your own body, below you in VR first person, moves in those pulses. On: the hero's body is drawn under your neck the whole time, moving as smoothly as you do, while the game's hero catches up under it. Only what is drawn moves: where the hero really is, what hits him, his walking and everything else stay the game's (a blocked hero's body may be drawn up to the limit below past a wall). Off: the body is drawn where the game's hero is, as before. Live.
openxr.roomscale_cap_m.label = Room-scale walking: the farthest the view leaves a blocked hero, m
openxr.roomscale_cap_m.tip = When the hero cannot follow (a wall, a monster, a door) and you walk on, the view goes ahead of him at most this far; past it the room slides with you - the view stays this far from him, without a jump. Step back and he walks under your head again. Live.
openxr.direct_input.label = Controls without BodyWalk (the plugin reads the controllers itself)
openxr.direct_input.tip = Native OpenXR only. The plugin reads the sticks, triggers, grips and buttons of both controllers and gives the game its own gamepad, actions and key commands - BodyWalk is not needed for the controls. While this is on, BodyWalk's gamepad buttons, gestures and actions are ignored (it can stay on for FlatVR); its walking is the exception, see the box below. Layout: the left stick walks, the right stick turns; the right trigger attacks, A picks up or opens, B / X / Y are the gamepad's skill buttons (left trigger held: the second row), the right stick click swaps weapons, the left stick click shows items (Alt) and, as a quick click, the map, the menu button opens the inventory (held for half a second: the game's pause menu, Esc; on PS VR2 the menu button is the Options button of the RIGHT controller); in a menu the controllers are the game's own gamepad (A B X Y, the grips are the bumpers) and the laser works as before. Change any of it in the lists under Controls > Buttons of the controllers, or in d2r_vr.ini, section [direct]. Off: BodyWalk's controls, as before. F4 only: in F1, F2, F3 and the flat modes BodyWalk's controls are the controls, as if this were off - except the controllers in F1-F3 when BodyWalk is not running (the box "Play with the controllers in F1, F2, F3 without BodyWalk" below).
direct.flat_controller.label = Play with the controllers in F1, F2, F3 without BodyWalk
direct.flat_controller.tip = VR views F1 (from above), F2 (third person) and F3 (the game on the floor) with no BodyWalk running: the plugin's own controllers are the game's gamepad there - the same layout as first person (F4): the right trigger attacks, A picks up or opens, B / X / Y are the gamepad's skill buttons (left trigger held: the second row), the right stick click swaps weapons, the left stick click shows items (Alt) and, as a quick click, the map, the menu button opens the inventory (the pause menu's long press is F4's), the sticks are the gamepad's (the left one walks the hero, the left trigger + a flick of a stick drinks a belt potion, see the boxes below); in a menu they are the game's own gamepad. Rebind in d2r_vr.ini, section [direct] (the same lines as F4). What stays F4 only: gestures, hit by touch, the bow's draw, throws, the skill wheel and aiming by the hand (in F1 and F3 the hero attacks where he faces). With BodyWalk running (its Game Link alive, or its gamepad moving) nothing changes: BodyWalk's gamepad is the gamepad, whole. If a real gamepad answers as well, the controllers are added to it, never over it. Off: no buttons from the controllers in F1-F3 without BodyWalk (the walk and the potions only). The log says "the plugin's own controller is the game's pad" when it takes over. Live.
direct.flatvr_controls.label = FlatVR: the controllers by this layout (BodyWalk's Mapping not needed)
direct.flatvr_controls.tip = In FlatVR the controllers work as in native OpenXR: BodyWalk hands the controllers to the game as they are (Game Link, BodyWalk with raw controls - 1.83 with the D2R VR link), and the layout above - the buttons, the triggers, the sticks, rebindable in Controls > Buttons of the controllers - and everything of first person (the belt, gestures, the bow, the quivers, the shoulders, the pause menu) runs on them. BodyWalk's Mapping and its gamepad are not read at all then (Game Link direct: no double presses); in F1, F2, F3 the controllers act as without BodyWalk (the box above). BodyWalk's walk comes through Game Link - its Output "Game Link" (BodyWalk's Engine: FlatVR + D2R VR) - into the controllers' stick (the box "BodyWalk's walking still walks the hero"). The camera and the arms keep BodyWalk's head and hands, as before. An older BodyWalk sends no raw controllers: its Mapping stays the controls (the log says so). Status says "BodyWalk: Game Link direct". Off: BodyWalk's Mapping and gamepad in FlatVR, as before. Live.
direct.hold_enabled.label = Long presses: stick click (right = skill panel, left = inventory), left menu button = pause menu
direct.hold_enabled.tip = With the controls above: hold the right stick's click for half a second and the skill panel opens (the wheel, when it is set to open that way); hold the left stick's click and the inventory opens - or closes, the button is a toggle; hold the left menu button (PS VR2: the right controller's Options) and the game gets Esc, its pause menu (the box "Pause menu (Esc)" in Controls > Buttons of the controllers). A short click is what it was: the right stick swaps weapons (when you let go), the left one shows the items (Alt), the menu button opens the inventory (when you let go). In d2r_vr.ini [direct]: hold_ms for the time, right_stick_hold, left_stick_hold and left_menu_hold for what they do (any button can have a long press: Controls > Buttons of the controllers). Off: a click acts the moment it is pressed, there are no long presses (and so no pause button, unless you put the pause menu on a plain button in that list).
direct.hold_stick_max_pct.label = Long press of a stick only with the stick centred: most lean, %
direct.hold_stick_max_pct.tip = A stick's click counts as a long press (the inventory, the skill panel) only while that stick leans no further than this. Pushed further - walking or turning in a fight and pressing it by accident - holding the click opens nothing. A quick click is still its tap at any lean: running, the map opens without stopping. 0 = no limit, as before. Live.
direct.left_stick_map.label = Quick click of the left stick: show / hide the map
direct.left_stick_map.tip = With the controls above: a short click of the left thumbstick shows or hides the map (the same as the left grip with the menu button). Held, the left click is still Alt (show items); held for half a second it is the inventory (see above). Off: the left click is Alt only, as before. F4 only, like the rest of the controls. Live.
direct.walk_flat_views.label = Walk with the left stick in F1, F2, F3 too (movement only)
direct.walk_flat_views.tip = F1-F3: movement. With the controls above, the left thumbstick also walks the hero in the other VR views - from above (F1), third person (F2) and the table (F3) - when BodyWalk is not running (the buttons are the box above; gestures, panels and vibration stay F4 only). The walk is the game's own: the same walking code, dead zone and stop BodyWalk's stick uses, the stick turned into the game's frame the way BodyWalk's stick is in that view (F1 from above: forward is up on the screen). Panels and menus keep the stick for themselves. BodyWalk running (its Game Link alive): nothing changes, its gamepad is the gamepad whole, as before. Off: F1-F3 have no walking without BodyWalk, as before. The log (d2r-vr-vrcam.log) says "walking in VR F1-F3 - ..." and why when it does not walk. Live.
direct.belt_flick_flat_views.label = Belt potions in F1, F2, F3: left trigger + a flick of a stick
direct.belt_flick_flat_views.tip = F1-F3: potions. With the controls above, in the other VR views - from above (F1), third person (F2) and the table (F3) - hold the LEFT TRIGGER and flick a thumbstick (either one): LEFT drinks belt column 1, UP column 2, RIGHT column 3, DOWN column 4 - the game's own belt keys 1-4, the same press the hand makes when it drinks a potion from the belt. One flick, one potion: bring the stick back to the middle before the next one; a stick that was already pushed when you pressed the trigger does nothing until it has been to the middle. While the trigger is held the left stick does not walk (the hero stops, so a flick never walks him). The trigger alone does nothing. Works only without BodyWalk (BodyWalk running: its own buttons, nothing changes). First person (F4) is not touched: there the trigger and the sticks are the layout's. Off: no potions from the sticks in F1-F3. The log says "belt flick - ..." for each potion and why a flick was not taken. Live.
openxr.direct_bodywalk_walk.label = BodyWalk's walking still walks the hero (with the controllers' stick)
openxr.direct_bodywalk_walk.tip = With the controls above: BodyWalk walks by the motion of your body - steps in place, an arm swing, a lean - and turns it into a walking stick. On: BodyWalk is still given your head and hands (never a button or a stick of the controllers: it presses nothing a second time) and ITS LEFT STICK, nothing else of its gamepad, walks the hero through the game's own walking code, mixed into the controller's left stick: each counts past the game's dead zone, together they add up (never past a full stick), and when they pull in opposite ways the stronger one wins. Panels and menus keep the controller's stick for themselves. Off: BodyWalk's walking is ignored with the rest of its input in direct mode, and BodyWalk is given no headset (as before). BodyWalk must be running and write its gamepad (Input Source: Game Link). The log (d2r-vr-vrcam.log) says "BodyWalk's walk - combined / ignored / dropped" and why. F4 only: in F1, F2, F3 BodyWalk's gamepad is the gamepad whole, as before. Live.
openxr.skill_wheel.label = Skill wheel: the controller's skill slots in the headset
openxr.skill_wheel.tip = Native OpenXR only. A wheel of the controller's eight skill slots (the gamepad's B, X, Y, RB and the same four with the left trigger held) in front of you. Open it: hold the grip of the hand that does not point (the left one with the right laser hand) and click the pointing hand's thumbstick. Point a wedge with the laser and pull the trigger: from then on that hand's trigger casts the slot - the game's own gamepad button, with its own animation, mana and cooldown. The centre is the basic attack again. EDIT SKILLS -> a slot -> a skill assigns a learned skill to the slot, through the game's own setter and checked back. Names are the game's own text; for icons run tools/skill_icons/prepare_skill_icons.py once (it reads YOUR installed game; nothing of it ships), without them the wheel shows names. Off: nothing of it exists.
openxr.skill_wheel_open.label = Skill panel opens by
openxr.skill_wheel_open.tip = How you open (and close) the skill panel. Long press of the right stick: hold the right thumbstick's click for about half a second (a short click is still the weapon swap) - needs "Controls without BodyWalk"; the same long press closes it. Left grip + right stick click: hold the grip of the hand that does not point and click the pointing hand's thumbstick. With the long press chosen but BodyWalk's input in use, the grip chord still works. Live.
openxr.skill_wheel_open.choice0 = Left grip + right stick click
openxr.skill_wheel_open.choice1 = Long press of the right stick
openxr.skill_panel_style.label = Skill panel style
openxr.skill_panel_style.tip = How the skill panel looks. Wheel: a ring of eight wedges. Tiles: a window made like the game's own skill dialog - two rows of six copper plates (A X B Y RB RT, and the same six with the left trigger held), red where a slot holds a skill, the pad button's mark under each (and, with "Controls without BodyWalk" on, the controller button that presses it); EDIT SKILLS shows every skill you have as a grid of plates. The same trigger cast, the same editor; only the look. Live.
openxr.skill_panel_style.choice0 = Wheel
openxr.skill_panel_style.choice1 = Tiles
openxr.skill_wheel_distance_m.label = Skill panel: distance, m
openxr.skill_wheel_distance_m.tip = How far in front of your head the wheel or the tiles hang when they open. Live.
openxr.skill_wheel_width_m.label = Skill wheel: width, m
openxr.skill_wheel_width_m.tip = How wide the wheel is (it is square). Live.
openxr.skill_tiles_width_m.label = Skill tiles: width, m
openxr.skill_tiles_width_m.tip = How wide the tiles' window is (its height follows). Live.
openxr.skill_categories.label = Skill editor: categories (All, the class's skill trees, General / Items)
openxr.skill_categories.tip = EDIT SKILLS -> a slot: a strip over the list of skills with the tabs All, your class's three skill trees (named as the game names them, in your language) and General / Items (the town portal, the basic attack, a skill an item gives), each with its count. Which tree a skill is on comes from the game's own tables, read once by tools/skill_icons/prepare_skill_icons.py (run it again after updating the mod, an older icon cache has no trees: then there is only the one list). Off: the one list of every skill, as before. Live. Idea after bearstonem/d2r-pcvr (MIT).
openxr.skill_panel_edit_first.label = Skill panel opens ready to edit: tap a slot to change its skill
openxr.skill_panel_edit_first.tip = The skill panel's first page edits: point at a slot and pull the trigger, and the list of your skills comes up - pick one and the game puts it on that slot (as EDIT SKILLS -> a slot does; the button is still there). Before, a tap on a slot picked it for the trigger - from then on the trigger cast that slot's skill; that is now the trigger HELD half a second on the slot. Unticked: as before - a tap picks the slot for the trigger, EDIT SKILLS edits. Live. F4 only.
openxr.skill_run_walk.label = Skill panel: a RUN / WALK button
openxr.skill_run_walk.tip = A RUN / WALK button on the skill panel's first page (a tile beside the first row in Tiles, a button in the footer of the Wheel). Pointing at it and pulling the trigger presses the game's own run / walk command, the one on the controller, and the panel stays open; it shows which one the game is on now. Off (the default): no button - put the command on a button of yours instead: Controls > Buttons of the controllers (and the headset's Left / Right pages) offer "Run / walk switch", and BodyWalk's bindings offer "D2R key: Run / walk switch". Live. Idea after bearstonem/d2r-pcvr (MIT).
openxr.skill_rt_a.label = Skill panel: skills on the right trigger and on A
openxr.skill_rt_a.tip = In first person, with the controls driven by the mod (direct input): the right trigger casts the skill on the game's RT slot and the right A the skill on its A slot - the game's own buttons, so its mana, cooldown and animation - and with the left trigger held, LT + RT and LT + A. Put a skill on them in the panel's EDIT SKILLS (the Tiles look): point at the RT or A plate, pick a skill; pick "Attack" there to put the slot back. A slot with nothing, Attack or Interact on it leaves its control as it is today (the trigger is the attack, A interacts). A slot you picked on the panel's first page still owns the trigger. Hit by touch's "the trigger no longer attacks" withholds only the plain attack: a skill on RT casts. Off (the default): the trigger and A are what the layout makes of them. Live.
openxr.runtime_fov.label = Each eye exactly as the headset gives it
openxr.runtime_fov.tip = Native OpenXR: how each eye is handed to the headset. A streamer such as ALVR (an Apple Vision Pro), or a layer, shows only the headset's own view right: with our own view the world is cross-eyed or stretched in the game while it looks right with SteamVR's menu up.\nCentred (the default): each eye is drawn centred, as wide and as tall each way as the headset's widest and tallest side (after bearstonem/d2r-pcvr) - the game's lighting, shadows, reflections and the names over monsters stay right - and only the headset's own part of it goes to the headset, an image of its own with exactly the headset's view (about a fifth of the width and a tenth of the height is drawn and not shown).\nThe headset's own angles: each eye drawn off-centre with exactly the headset's angles and handed in whole - what "Set each eye's angles by hand" with the headset's own numbers does. Every pixel is shown, but the game draws its interface once for both eyes, so the names over monsters and items can come apart, and some effects can differ between the eyes.\nOff: our own view, below. With frame generation on (Home), Centred does nothing (the headset went black with the two together). The picture is stretched to the window's shape (Resolution: "Use the headset's recommended size" keeps it sharp). Live.
openxr.runtime_fov.choice0 = Off: our own view (the choices below)
openxr.runtime_fov.choice1 = Centred, each eye's own part handed in
openxr.runtime_fov.choice2 = The headset's own angles, drawn off-centre
openxr.symmetric_fov.label = Labels over monsters meet in both eyes
openxr.symmetric_fov.tip = Each eye drawn as wide to the left as to the right: the game's interface (the names over monsters and items) is the same in both eyes and meets. Off: each eye's own view, a little fewer pixels, the names apart.
openxr.fov_crop.label = Sharper: the picture keeps the window's shape
openxr.fov_crop.tip = Each eye's view cut to the game window's shape: square pixels, all the window's lines on a smaller angle, so the picture is sharper; above and below it the headset shows black (nothing drawn there, it costs nothing). Off: the picture stretched over the headset's whole view - taller, softer up and down.
openxr.fov_override.label = Set each eye's angles by hand
openxr.fov_override.tip = For headsets or streamers whose picture stays distorted (e.g. an Apple Vision Pro via ALVR: the world cross-eyed or stretched while it looks right with SteamVR's menu up). On: each eye is drawn with the four angles below and handed to the headset with exactly them, the whole picture - "Each eye exactly as the headset gives it" and the two choices under it do nothing. Start from the headset's own angles (the button), then turn the sliders with the game running until the world looks right - the picture changes at once - and tell us the numbers, so we can make them automatic. The angles are the LEFT eye's, from the middle of its view: outer = to the left, inner = towards the nose; the right eye gets their mirror. Off (the default): the headset's own angles.
openxr.fov_outer.label = Angle: outer (deg)
openxr.fov_outer.tip = How far each eye's view reaches to its outer side (the left eye's left, the right eye's right), in degrees from the middle. Live.
openxr.fov_inner.label = Angle: inner (deg)
openxr.fov_inner.tip = How far each eye's view reaches towards the nose, in degrees from the middle. Live.
openxr.fov_up.label = Angle: up (deg)
openxr.fov_up.tip = How far each eye's view reaches up, in degrees from the middle. Live.
openxr.fov_down.label = Angle: down (deg)
openxr.fov_down.tip = How far each eye's view reaches down, in degrees from the middle. Live.
@run.fov_from_headset.label = Set the sliders to the headset's own angles
@run.fov_from_headset.tip = Copies the angles the headset's runtime gave at the game's last headset session (the line below) into the four sliders.
openxr.ipd_auto.label = Eye distance: from the headset
openxr.ipd_auto.tip = On (the default): the distance between the two eyes of the stereo picture is what the headset's runtime says (the position of each eye's view). Off: the number of your own below - the two eyes keep their middle and their turns and stand that far apart. Use it when the headset's was not picked up (a runtime that puts both eyes in one place gets 64 mm: the line below says what it reports) or was picked up wrong: the world looks too small / too big, or two images do not merge. Your IPD is on the headset's wheel or in its software too (the picture there is the headset's own); this is the distance the GAME's two cameras are drawn at. Native OpenXR only, live; FlatVR has its own (Stereo > Scale and depth).
openxr.ipd_mm.label = Eye distance, mm
openxr.ipd_mm.tip = The distance between your eyes in millimetres (about 63 for an adult; the headset's own is the line below). The game's two cameras are drawn this far apart, about the middle of your head. Live.
openxr.canted_eyes.label = Canted displays: both eyes in the head's frame
openxr.canted_eyes.tip = For headsets whose two displays are turned outward (Pimax, Varjo, Valve Index and some others). The game's camera is one view for both eyes, but each eye used to be handed to the headset with its own turn, so on such a headset the eyes came out crossed and the centre stretched (until a Steam menu was opened over the game). On: when the headset's two views differ by more than a quarter of a degree both eyes are drawn and handed over in the head's frame, each with the frustum that covers its own view (the headset turns them to its displays). Headsets with parallel displays are not touched. Off: as before. Live. The game's log says whether yours are canted ("each eye's own view from the head's frame").
@window.square.label = Square game window (no black bars)
@window.square.tip = In VR (native OpenXR or FlatVR): writes the game's own Settings.json, a window, as wide as it is tall (the size below). The headset's eye is about square, so the whole picture fills it - no black bars with the box above ticked. vrcam keeps the window square while the game runs (the game writes a cut size back into its file). The window you had is kept first; in flat mode (Home > How you play) there is no square: the game uses the window and resolution you set in its own options, and your window comes back at once. Off: the size it had before.
openxr.window_size.label = Square window: size, px
openxr.window_size.tip = The square window's side, as far as a monitor holds it (past a monitor's edge the game itself closes): about 2060 on a 4K screen. Bigger: make a virtual monitor that size in BodyWalk (Virtual Monitor, no need to make it primary) - vrcam moves the game's window onto it by itself. Bigger is sharper and slower.
@status.square_window.label = The game window as the game has it
openxr.third_gaze.label = F2: the camera swings round the hero with the gaze
openxr.third_gaze.tip = Off: the camera stays behind the hero on his turn and the head looks round freely. On: it swings round him with the head, as on FlatVR's screen.
openxr.haptics.label = Controller vibration
openxr.haptics.tip = A short pulse in the hand when a blow of yours lands, a belt potion is taken or drunk, the laser clicks on a menu, or you pick something up or open it. The game itself is not changed - the pulses only watch. Native OpenXR only (the headset's runtime drives the motors); off: silent, as before. Live. F4 only.
openxr.haptics_scale.label = Vibration: strength
openxr.haptics_scale.tip = All pulses stronger or weaker; 1 = the usual (a landed blow is about 70% of the motor's strength). Live.
openxr.frame_profile.label = Steam Frame controllers: their own layout
openxr.frame_profile.tip = Native OpenXR. When the runtime offers the Steam Frame's controllers as themselves (XR_VALVE_frame_controller_interaction), they get their own buttons instead of the runtime's stand-in for a Quest or an Index controller: the right A and B as before, the left hand's D-pad down and up are its first and second face buttons (X and Y on a Quest controller), the left View and the right Menu buttons are the menu. Other controllers and runtimes without it: nothing changes. Taken when the headset session starts. Off: the runtime's stand-in layout, as before.
openxr.index_grip_force.label = Valve Index: the grip is how hard you squeeze
openxr.index_grip_force.tip = Native OpenXR, Valve Index controllers. The Index reads its grip from the fingers round the handle, so a relaxed hand that only holds the controller counts as a squeezed grip (a weapon or a potion taken, the laser's Shift). On: the grip is the handle's force sensor - only a real squeeze counts. Other controllers: nothing changes. Live. Off: as before.
openxr.haptics_hand_actions.label = Vibration: a channel of its own for each hand
openxr.haptics_hand_actions.tip = Each controller's motor gets a vibration action of its own, so a pulse can only go to the hand it is for (some runtimes sent a pulse of the shared action to the wrong hand). Taken when the headset session starts. Off: one action for both hands, as before.
openxr.haptics_stop.label = Vibration: stop each pulse on time
openxr.haptics_stop.tip = Each pulse is stopped by its own call when its time is up, even while the game is loading or stalls - some controllers (Steam Frame's) went on buzzing past a short pulse. Live. Off: the runtime ends a pulse by itself, as before.

# --- Stereo 3D ---
group.stereo_3d = Stereo 3D
group.stereo_3d.help = How the two eyes are drawn: real stereo, both eyes from one game frame, and the eyes-by-turns fixes (the other eye made from the depth, ghosts, rims). Tick Swap eyes if the depth looks inside out.
stereo.afr.label = Real stereo (alternate frames)
stereo.afr.tip = The game draws the left eye, the right eye, the left... Needs the FlatVR addon in the game, FlatVR picture source = UEVR (full-size SBS), VSync off and a high frame cap (180 fps = 90 per eye).
stereo.pair_per_tick.label = Both eyes from one game frame
stereo.pair_per_tick.tip = The frame is drawn twice (left, then right with the game time held) instead of one eye per frame by turns. Same pairs per second; the game itself updates half as often.
stereo.turn_warp.label = Eyes by turns: make the other eye from the depth
stereo.turn_warp.tip = Native OpenXR with the eyes by turns: the eye not drawn this frame is made on the graphics card for where the head is now - its own last picture moved with the depth it was drawn with (what the hero holds goes with him), at this frame's pose. Unticked: it goes to the headset as it was last drawn, and the headset turns it (rotation only: a step or a moving monster shows a frame behind in that eye). First person (F4) only. Live. Idea: bearstonem/d2r-pcvr.
stereo.turn_from_drawn.label = ... with the eye drawn this frame over it
stereo.turn_from_drawn.tip = The eye drawn this frame is moved across to the other eye with its own depth and laid over its older picture, so what moves by itself - monsters, missiles - stands where it is now in both eyes; behind an edge, what that eye could not see, the older picture shows. Unticked: the other eye's own last picture alone. Live.
stereo.turn_overlay_hide.label = ... its overlays hidden by its moved depth
stereo.turn_overlay_hide.tip = The depth is moved with the other eye's picture too, to the pixel, and what the effect draws over it - the wrist medallions, the bow's orbs - is hidden there where that picture shows a hand or the bow nearer. Unticked: nothing of the scene hides them in that eye - they show through the hands every second frame of each eye. Live.
stereo.turn_fx_fence.label = Eyes by turns: each frame's effects wait for the last frame's
stereo.turn_fx_fence.tip = Each frame's effects (the sky, the fog) wait until the graphics card is past the last frame's effects and the other eye's overlays before their cameras go in. ReShade keeps one buffer of them per effect, and while the card was a frame behind the next frame overwrote it: the sky was drawn with the next frame's head turn and shook in both eyes. Unticked: no wait. Live.
stereo.turns_keep_own.label = ... the other eye's own picture kept
stereo.turns_keep_own.tip = Where the other eye's own older picture, moved with its depth, shows the same surface as the eye drawn this frame, it stays: the game's glow round a blade, hair and its effects (spells, flames, Tyrael's wings) have no depth, and moved across from the eye drawn they stood where that eye saw them - a ghost blade, a second outline, the scene through the wings. Where the game's effects are (the default, bearstonem/d2r-pcvr's owner's choice at Tyrael): the wings right everywhere. Round near things: the hands, the weapon, a monster close by. Everywhere: that eye a frame behind the other all over (grass, flames, monsters' motion). Nowhere: the eye drawn's picture wherever it reaches, as before. Live.
stereo.turns_keep_own.choice0 = Nowhere
stereo.turns_keep_own.choice1 = Round near things
stereo.turns_keep_own.choice2 = Everywhere
stereo.turns_keep_own.choice3 = Where the game's effects are (default)
stereo.turns_keep_own.choice4 = Near things and effects
stereo.turns_rims.label = ... the dark rims round roofs and trees go with them
stereo.turns_rims.tip = The game draws anything against the sky a pixel larger than its depth: a dark rim beside every roof, treetop and far building. Moved with the sky's depth, that rim stayed where the eye drawn saw it while the roof moved across: a dark, ragged outline beside it in every other frame of each eye. Ticked: within 2 pixels of something, the sky takes its depth, so the rim goes with it. Unticked: as before. Live. From bearstonem/d2r-pcvr.
stereo.turns_fill.label = ... no frame-old ghosts beside near things
stereo.turns_fill.tip = Beside anything near, the other eye sees a strip the eye drawn this frame could not, and it keeps its own picture of a frame ago there - a monster that has moved since was left in it, a ghost beside it in one eye. Ticked: where that older picture is nearer than what is behind the strip, what is behind beside it fills the strip instead. Unticked: as before. Live. From bearstonem/d2r-pcvr.
stereo.turns_sharp.label = ... the other eye read sharper
stereo.turns_sharp.tip = The other eye's picture, turned and moved, lands between the pixels it was drawn with. Read the usual way each step averages two of them, and fine detail and text went softer every other frame in each eye. Ticked: a sharper read (Catmull-Rom) that keeps more of it, without rings round edges. Unticked: as before. Live. From bearstonem/d2r-pcvr.
stereo.right_dt_ms.label = Right eye frame time, ms
stereo.right_dt_ms.tip = The right eye's pass gets this much game time instead of none. Effects that skip a frame of no time (butterflies only in the left eye) are drawn then; 0.01 is enough, more moves the world between the eyes.
stereo.props_once_a_pair.label = Hanging lanterns move once a pair (F4)
stereo.props_once_a_pair.tip = Props the game swings - hanging lanterns, chains, signs - are stepped in the left eye's pass only, and both eyes get that pose. Where the right eye is drawn by a second pass (no replay, or before the replay starts in a new area) they were stepped again with the tiny right-eye time and twitched. VR F4 only; the other views as before. Idea: bearstonem/d2r-pcvr. Off: as before.
render.fx_fence.label = Effects: each eye's values exactly its own
render.fx_fence.tip = The effects (fog, sky, ceiling) wait until the graphics card has drawn the last eye's effects before the next eye's values go in. Both eyes of a pair get the same values anyway; this matters for FlatVR's frame stamps with one picture a frame. Costs a little speed. Live. F4 only.
stereo.swap.label = Swap eyes
stereo.swap.tip = Tick if the eyes come out swapped (depth looks inside out).
stereo.pace_flatvr_only.label = Hold frames to the headset only while FlatVR runs
stereo.pace_flatvr_only.tip = In FlatVR modes the plugin holds the game's pictures to the headset's rate so FlatVR gets them evenly. With FlatVR (BodyWalk) not running nothing takes them: ticked, the game then runs as fast as it can. Unticked: held to the headset's rate always, as before. Live.

# --- Scale and depth ---
group.scale_and_depth = Scale and depth
group.scale_and_depth.help = How big the world feels and how strong the 3D is with FlatVR: Life-size world takes it from the FlatVR screen and your height; otherwise set the eye separation and the depth behind the screen by hand.
stereo.true_scale.label = Life-size world
stereo.true_scale.tip = Eye distance and the screen plane from the FlatVR screen and your height. The two sliders below it are then unused.
stereo.eye_mm.label = My eye distance, mm
stereo.ipd.label = Eye separation
stereo.ipd.tip = World units (the hero is ~7.5 tall, so 0.27 is about 6.4 cm). More = stronger 3D.
stereo.convergence.label = Depth behind the screen
stereo.convergence.tip = The distance that sits on the FlatVR screen; farther goes deeper behind it. 0 = parallel eyes (everything in front of the screen). Smaller = deeper.

# --- Timing ---
group.timing = Timing
group.timing.help = How FlatVR places and picks each frame: frame stamps, the newest finished picture and the pipeline depth. Change these if head turns judder or double.
stereo.stamps.label = Frame stamps (FlatVR places each frame at its head pose)
stereo.stamps.tip = Each frame tells FlatVR when its view was taken, so the screen sits where the head was then. Untick if tabletop or first person judders or doubles when you turn your head - FlatVR then keeps the screen at the head as it is, like in the other views. Takes effect at once.
stereo.picture_ring.label = Newest finished picture (FlatVR frame ring)
stereo.picture_ring.tip = FlatVR takes the newest picture the game has finished instead of the one shared picture. Off by default: with it head turns in tabletop and first person juddered (FlatVR addon 2.19 and newer). Takes effect within a second.
stereo.pipeline_depth.label = Pipeline depth (smoother head turns)
stereo.pipeline_depth.tip = How many of an eye's views the shown frame lags the newest one. Try 0, 1 and 2 for the smoothest head turn.

# --- FlatVR like native OpenXR ---
group.flatvr_like_native_openxr = FlatVR like native OpenXR
group.flatvr_like_native_openxr.help = FlatVR only: each picture starts on FlatVR's next frame with the head FlatVR hands out, as native OpenXR does, so walking, the hands and animations no longer jerk. Off: our own timer, as before.
flatvr.frame_sync.label = FlatVR: pictures on FlatVR's frames
flatvr.frame_sync.tip = FlatVR only (no native session). Each picture starts on FlatVR's next frame, with the head FlatVR hands out then - as native OpenXR starts each pair on the headset's own wait. Before, the game ran on a timer of ours and its own frame cap while FlatVR showed at the headset's rate: the pictures came 1, 2, 1, 1, 2 times each and walking, the hands and animations jerked. A pair that takes longer than a headset frame goes on every other frame (an even 45 of 90, as a runtime halves a game that misses) - or, with the third choice, on every new head (more pictures, unevenly). The game's own frame cap is written as twice the rate then (only a stop for a game running away). No head from FlatVR: our timer as before. Live.
flatvr.frame_sync.choice0 = Off - our own timer (as before)
flatvr.frame_sync.choice1 = On - every other frame when a pair does not fit (even)
flatvr.frame_sync.choice2 = On - every frame FlatVR has a head for
flatvr.frame_sync_late.label = FlatVR frames: a head is late after, share of a frame
flatvr.frame_sync_late.tip = A head from FlatVR older than this share of a frame when the last pair ends is let go and the next one waited for. Live.
flatvr.head_level.label = FlatVR: the horizon is the real horizon
flatvr.head_level.tip = FlatVR, F4 only. The camera's pitch and roll are the headset's own against gravity, as in native OpenXR. Before, the camera's pitch was the game's camera plus [camera] pitch plus the head's pitch since the last F11: any amount apart from the head turned into a lean of the world on every head turn (FlatVR hangs the picture at the head's full pose), and BodyWalk's roll came out too small when looking up or down. Off: as before. Live.
flatvr.head_position.label = FlatVR: the camera moves with your head
flatvr.head_position.tip = FlatVR, F4 only. Leaning, crouching, a step aside move the camera as far in the game (at the hero's size), from where the head was at the last recentre (F11) - as native OpenXR does. Off: turns only, and the world moves along with the head when it leans. Live.
flatvr.room_centre.label = FlatVR: one centre with BodyWalk
flatvr.room_centre.tip = FlatVR. Straight ahead is taken from the room FlatVR places its screen in, at our recentre (F11). BodyWalk's own Reset Center (its button or key) no longer turns the world away from FlatVR's screen: it recentres the game too. Off: as before (after BodyWalk's reset an F11 was needed). Live.
flatvr.recenter_on_enter.label = FlatVR: straight ahead when a game starts
flatvr.recenter_on_enter.tip = FlatVR. When the hero appears (a game entered), straight ahead is where you look then - as native OpenXR does. Off: straight ahead stays where it was (where the headset looked when BodyWalk started, or the last F11).

hud.labels_near.label = Labels nearer / farther

hud_top.pointer_top.label = Mouse pointer depth: top of the screen

hud_top.pointer_mid.label = Mouse pointer depth: middle
hud_top.pointer_bottom.label = Mouse pointer depth: bottom of the screen
hud_top.pointer_top_size.label = Mouse pointer size at the top, %

hud_floor.map_size.label = Map size, %
hud_floor.map_size.tip = The corner map (Tab) smaller or larger, about its own corner. Needs D2R_DepthFog.fx on in ReShade (it draws the map back); without it the game's own map stays. The mouse pointer lies on the game's ground by itself here.
hud_floor.map_near.label = Map nearer / farther
hud_floor.map_near.tip = Real stereo only: + brings the map towards the eyes, - pushes it behind the screen; 0 = where the game puts it.
hud_floor.map_x.label = Map left / right, %
hud_floor.map_x.tip = The map moved across the screen, % of the screen's width: + right, - left; 0 = its corner, where the game puts it.
hud_floor.map_y.label = Map up / down, %
hud_floor.map_y.tip = The map moved up the screen, % of the screen's height: + up (partly off the screen), - down; 0 = the top, where the game puts it.

# --- Item labels on the ground ---

hud_floor.labels_alpha.tip = How much of the dark box behind the names of items on the ground is drawn: 1 = as the game draws it, 0 = no box, the names alone. The names themselves stay bright. Should the game's label code not be found (another game build), the labels are faded as a picture by D2R_DepthFog.fx instead: the boxes fade, the names stay. Only on the floor (F3).
hud_floor.labels_size.tip = The names of items on the ground and their boxes, smaller or larger, each about the point under it; the game makes room for them at that size. 100 = the game's own. Through the game's label code: on another game build it does nothing (vrcam's log says so). Only on the floor (F3); item tooltips and every other text keep their size.

body.flat_hold_trunk.label = Keep the body under the camera when attacking

input.portal_auto.label = Walk into a portal to enter it
input.portal_auto.tip = Third and first person with W A S D: walk up to a town portal with a move key held and it takes you - the game's own click on the portal, made for you once the game shows the portal under the pointer. You are not sent back through the portal you came out of: walk away from it first. From sajmonsoft's flat fork. Off = click the portal as before.

# --- Menus ---
group.menus = Menus
group.menus.help = How you use menus and panels in VR first person (F4). The laser pointer makes a controller the mouse; you can also see item tooltips at once, keep the world in 3D around a menu panel, move a panel nearer or farther with right grip + stick, and open a settings panel in the headset.
openxr.laser.label = Laser pointer on menus and panels (prototype)
openxr.laser.tip = Point a controller at the flat picture of the menus, the inventory, the stash or a trader and it is the mouse: the trigger clicks, with the grip held it right-clicks, a held trigger drags. The other hand's trigger is Ctrl (an item to the stash or the trader), its grip Shift. While the laser points at the picture its triggers and grips are not BodyWalk's; a stick or A / B gives the panel back to the pad until you point somewhere else. The game stays in its controller layout. Not on F1 and F3.
openxr.laser_hand.label = Laser hand
openxr.laser_hand.tip = The hand the laser comes from; the other one's trigger and grip are Ctrl and Shift.
openxr.laser_tooltips.label = Item tooltips at once under the laser
openxr.laser_tooltips.tip = Pointing the laser at an item shows the game's own tooltip at once, with the comparison against the item you wear beside it - no 1000 ms wait for the tooltip and no Shift held for the comparison. It is the game's tooltip and the game's comparison, only earlier; Shift still buys stacks and moves items as before. Off: the game's delay, and Shift for the comparison. F4 only.
openxr.laser_typing.label = Typing on the keyboard works under the laser
openxr.laser_typing.tip = While the laser points at a menu the game is held in its controller layout, and in that layout its text boxes take no letters - nothing could be typed into D2RLoader's Host Game and Browse Games, a character's name or a password, even on a real keyboard. Ticked: a key pressed on the keyboard lets the game take its keyboard layout for a moment, so the box takes what you type; the thumbstick brings the controller back. The laser's own Ctrl, Shift and Esc never count. Unticked: as before. Live. From bearstonem/d2r-pcvr.
openxr.laser_grip_tap.label = Grip tap turns menu pages under the laser
openxr.laser_grip_tap.tip = In a menu the grips are the game's bumpers: they turn the pages of the tabbed menu (inventory, character, skills ... options), the stash and a trader. While the laser points at the menu it keeps the grips for the right click and Shift; with this on, a quick tap of a grip (no trigger pressed meanwhile) still turns the page - left back, right on. A grip held longer or used with a click stays the laser's. Off: a page only after a stick has given the menu back to the pad, as before. F4 only.
openxr.laser_fit_window.label = Keep the game window on its monitor for the laser
openxr.laser_fit_window.tip = The laser moves the real mouse cursor, and Windows never puts it off the desktop: a game window bigger than its monitor (the 1920 square on a 1080p or 1440p screen) left parts of the picture - the bottom, or the tabs at the top - out of the laser's reach, and a click under the taskbar went to the taskbar. On: the window is kept inside its monitor above the taskbar - with a render size it is made smaller to fit (the picture in the headset keeps its size), without one only moved. Off: the window stays where and as big as it is.
openxr.menu_3d.label = Menus as a panel, the world stays in 3D
openxr.menu_3d.tip = First person (F4), native OpenXR or FlatVR: opening the inventory, the stash, a trader, the skills or the game menu keeps the world in stereo around you, and the game's interface hangs in front of you as a panel of its own - where the flat picture stood (its width, the panels' distance), the world seen through wherever the menu leaves it. Native: the laser points at the panel. FlatVR: needs a BodyWalk that hangs it (an older one keeps the flat menus). Off: a menu shows the flat picture, as before. F1, F2 and F3 always do.
openxr.menu_zoom.label = Right grip + right stick: a panel nearer / farther
openxr.menu_zoom.tip = Native OpenXR, F4: with a panel of the game in front (the inventory, the stash, a trader, the waypoints...), hold the right grip and push the right stick forward to bring it nearer, back to send it farther; let go and it stays there - written to "Flat picture with a panel open: distance" ([screen] menu_distance_m). It stops where the panel stops being readable: nearer, part of it would be out of sight; farther, the headset's pixels would skip the game's text. While the grip is held the stick's forward / back is not the game's, and the grip's own press (the menu's right bumper, where the laser does not have it) comes when you let go without moving the panel. Off: as before.
openxr.menu_zoom_speed_mps.label = Panel nearer / farther: speed, m/s
openxr.menu_zoom_speed_mps.tip = How fast the panel moves with the right stick pushed all the way. Live.
openxr.hand_inventory.label = Inventory on the left hand outside town
openxr.hand_inventory.tip = Native OpenXR, F4, with the laser on: away from town the game's whole inventory window hangs on your LEFT hand instead of in front - cut out of the interface, held over the left controller like a tablet, turned to your eyes - and the left stick goes on walking the hero while it is open: it no longer moves the inventory's cursor (the RIGHT hand's laser is the mouse on it) and goes to the game's own walking. The small button beside it puts the inventory in front, full size, and back on the hand. Drag an item off it and let go: the inventory closes and the game drops it. The long press of the left stick click opens and closes it even while you walk. In town, or with another menu (a waypoint, the game menu), in front as before. The game locks its own walk while its inventory is open; the left stick then sends the stick's own walk command for it, with the game's run rules. Off: as before.
openxr.hand_inventory_width_m.label = Inventory on the hand: width, m
openxr.hand_inventory_width_m.tip = How wide the inventory window is on the left hand. Live.
openxr.hand_inventory_front.label = Inventory opens in front, full size
openxr.hand_inventory_front.tip = Away from town the inventory opens in front, full size, instead of on the left hand. The button beside the inventory sets this too: it opens the way you last left it, after a restart as well. Live.
openxr.headset_settings.label = Settings panel in the headset (prototype)
openxr.headset_settings.tip = Native OpenXR without BodyWalk's menus: hold the right stick click (the long press), and a small settings panel opens in front of you - the flat picture's distance and width, brightness, your height, the laser, the VR render size (Video page: presets and a slider; applying it makes the game rebuild its picture, a few seconds frozen) and Calibrate body (Body page: the T-pose measurement, started from the headset) and the game view F1 - F4 (F1 - F3 close the panel; back to F4 by the F4 key, D2R VR Authentic Settings > Home, or a view action in BodyWalk's mapping). Point a controller at it and pull the trigger; Apply writes only what you changed into d2r_vr.ini (the original is kept once as d2r_vr.ini.before-headset-menu; a change made elsewhere meanwhile is shown, not overwritten). With the skill panel in the Tiles look (Skill panel style: Tiles) these pages are its Settings tab, beside Skills: the right stick's long press opens the window on the tab it was last on. While it is open both controllers are the panel's: nothing of them reaches the game, and it never sends the game a click. The long press again, B / Y or Menu close it. Two grips held mean nothing (the old both-grips + click way is on the Debug tab). Off: no panel. F4 only.

group.belt_potions.help = The potions of your belt hang on the hero's hips as the game's own models (F4). Take one with the grip and tip it at your mouth to drink, throw it on the ground or to your mercenary. The sliders set where the belt hangs, a hand's reach, how a bottle sits in the hand and how it lights up.

hands.belt_models.tip = First person (F4): the potions in the belt's bottom row hang on the hero's hips as the game's own 3D models - lit, shaded and fogged like everything else (the game draws them). Off: as before.

hands.belt_models_ahead.tip = The arc's radius round the hero's middle, in parts of his eye height: less = closer to the body, more = farther out. Live.

hands.belt_models_up.tip = How high on the hero they hang, in parts of his eye height (0.57 = the hips). Live.
hands.belt_models_arc.label = Belt potions: degrees between them
hands.belt_models_arc.tip = How far round the body the four spread: degrees on the arc from one column to the next. Live.
hands.belt_models_across.label = Belt potions: right (+) / left (-)
hands.belt_models_across.tip = The whole belt shifted across the hero, in parts of his eye height: + to his right, - to his left. The headset settings panel's Belt page writes the same key. Live.

hands.belt_models_turn.tip = The arc of potions swung round the hero: + to his right, - to his left. The headset settings panel's Belt page writes the same key. Live.
hands.belt_models_scale.label = Belt potions: size
hands.belt_models_scale.tip = 1 = the size the game gives them on the ground. Live.
hands.belt_grab_cm.label = Belt potions: grab reach, cm
hands.belt_grab_cm.tip = How near a hand's palm must be to a potion to light it and take it with the grip. A wide reach steals the grip meant for the weapon: narrower, or the belt lower or farther to the side (the sliders above), and the weapon is yours again. The headset settings panel's Belt page writes the same key. Live.
hands.belt_grab.label = Belt potions: take them in the hand and drink
hands.belt_grab.tip = A hand at a bottle lights it (a see-through ball, the bottle a little larger); the grip takes it into the hero's hand. Brought to the mouth and tipped over it is drunk (the game's own belt key 1-4); let go anywhere else it goes back. Switch BodyWalk's belt zones off with it. Live.
belt.grab_nearest.label = Grip: the nearer of a belt potion and the weapon wins
belt.grab_nearest.tip = A grip press that could take a belt potion OR the weapon goes to the NEARER one: your palm's distance to the bottle against your fist's distance to the weapon (the shaft of a weapon your other hand holds - a staff, a two-hander, a crossbow, the second hand; one lying on the floor; the weapon stowed on your back). A tie goes to the weapon; a hand behind a shoulder is the weapon swap's. A potion is lit (the ball) and taken only when it is the nearer one; where the weapon is nearer no potion is lit and the weapon takes the grip. The log says, for every grip press, who took it and why. Unticked: as before - a potion in reach wins over the weapon. First person (F4). Live.
belt.grab_trigger.label = Take a belt potion with trigger + grip
belt.grab_trigger.tip = On: a belt potion is taken only with the trigger squeezed together with the grip. The grip alone never takes a potion - it goes to the weapon or the shoulder swap - and a bottle in reach is only lit (the ball), it does not keep the grip from the weapon. Needs the controller's trigger from direct input; without it the grip alone takes, as before. Off (the default): the grip alone takes a potion. Live.
belt.hold_takes_trigger.label = Bottle in hand: the triggers are not the game's
belt.hold_takes_trigger.tip = While a belt bottle is in a hand (taken, or being drunk) the controller's triggers do not reach the game: the LEFT one (whichever hand holds the bottle) - the game reads it as Shift on a belt key, and Shift + a belt key is not a drink, so a potion taken with trigger + grip was not drunk - and a right hand's own trigger (no attack out of a drink). A trigger taken stays out until you let it go. Unticked: the triggers pass on as before. First person (F4). Live.

hands.belt_glow.label = Glow: strength

hands.belt_empty_bottle.label = Belt potions: the drunk bottle stays in the hand, empty
hands.belt_empty_bottle.tip = After the drink (the game's own, as ever) the hand keeps the bottle, empty: its cork and the liquid are hidden where the model has them as parts of their own (the light healing potion's liquid; the cork, rope and metal round the neck of every potion - most potions have their colour in the glass itself, which stays). Let go, it falls with its weight and your hand's motion - throw it away - lies on the ground and goes after a while. Only drawn: nothing of the game's. If the game did not take the drink, there is no empty bottle. First person (F4). Live. Unticked: the bottle is gone at the mouth, as before.

hands.belt_empty_dark.label = Empty bottle: darker
hands.belt_empty_dark.tip = The emptied bottle's colour times 1 + this (the game's own highlight, the other way): -0.35 = a third darker, 0 = as it is. Live.

The game lays it on the ground round the HERO (its drop has no place to aim at), so the game's potion lies at your feet. If the game does not drop it, it goes back into the belt. Let go near its place on the belt, it goes back as before. Throwing potions (gas, explosive) keep their own throw. First person (F4). Live. Unticked: let go anywhere, it goes back on the belt.

A miss goes back on the belt (with "thrown on the ground, the game drops it" on: the game drops it). The log says "belt bottles - ... the mercenary". First person (F4). Live. Unticked: as before.

# --- Item labels on the ground ---
group.item_labels_on_the_ground.help#4 = The names of items on the ground in first person (F4): the box's opacity, their size, smaller far away, and their stereo depth, so each label sits at its own item instead of floating far off. The names over monsters are set in Monster plates.
hud.labels_alpha.tip = How much of the dark box behind the names of items on the ground is drawn in first person (F4): 1 = as the game draws it, 0 = no box, the names alone. The names stay bright. Through the game's label code (vrcam's log says "item-label hook in"); on another game build it does nothing here.
hud.labels_size.tip = The names of items on the ground and their boxes in first person (F4), smaller or larger, each about the point under it. 100 = the game's own. Item tooltips and all other text keep their size.
hud.labels_far.label = Item labels: size far away, % of the size above
hud.labels_far.tip = Nearer names larger, farther ones smaller, as signs in the room: the size above for an item 1.5 m away and nearer, this much of it for one 10 m away and farther, smoothly in between. 100 = the same size at any distance.
hud.labels_whole_eye.label = Item labels down to the bottom of the picture (test)
hud.labels_whole_eye.tip = The game drops the name of an item whose label would reach below its interface's height. Where the interface is smaller than the picture - a square or tall VR render size, Safe Screen - items low in the view, the one you look down at, have no name, with Show Items held too. Ticked: the labels are kept down to the bottom of the picture. Every view. A test of bearstonem/d2r-pcvr's fix: try it on and off. Live.
hud.labels_depth_body.label = Item labels: at their items, %
hud.labels_depth_body.tip = In stereo the game draws the labels on the same spot in both eyes - in the headset they float far off, not on their items. Here each label is set at its own item's depth, by the item's distance from you: 100 = exactly there, 0 = where the game leaves them. Their interface layer is taken out of the picture for it; the toolbar and the map stay.
hud.labels_near_body.label = Item labels: stereo depth on top, all
hud.labels_near_body.tip = Every label (and the rest of the interface left in the picture, chat) nearer (+) or farther (-) by the same amount, on top of the slider above. The name and bar over a monster have a depth of their own (Monster plates, below) - none of the item labels' settings touch them.

# --- Monster plates ---
group.monster_plates.help#3 = The name and health bar over the monster you target: opacity, size, smaller far away, height and stereo depth, so in F4 it sits at its monster. Plate over the monster's head keeps it a set gap over the head at any distance.
hud.monster_alpha.tip#2 = The name plate the game shows for the monster you target (box, frame and name alike): 1 = as the game draws it, 0 = gone. Every view. Needs D2R_DepthFog.fx on in ReShade.
hud.monster_size.label = Name over a monster: size, %
hud.monster_size.tip = That plate smaller or larger about its middle. 100 = the game's own. Every view.
hud.monster_far.label = Name over a monster: size far away, % of the size above
hud.monster_far.tip = First person (F4). Nearer plates larger, farther ones smaller, as the item labels (Item labels: size far away): the size above for a monster 1.5 m away and nearer, this much of it for one 10 m away and farther, smoothly in between. 100 = the same size at any distance. Live.
hud.monster_over_head.label = Plate over the monster's head (prototype)
hud.monster_over_head.tip = First person (F4). The name and health bar the game hangs over the monster you target stay the game's own - nothing is cut out or drawn again - but are lifted (or lowered) so that their lower edge hangs the gap below over the monster's head, whatever the distance. The game's own gap is the same few pixels at any distance: some 7 cm over a head 1.5 m away, 45 cm over one 10 m away. The plate stays centred over the monster, as the game draws it. While on it replaces the height slider. Needs the game's controller layout (the one D2R VR plays in). Off: the plate where the game puts it. Live.
hud.monster_bar_gap_cm.label = Plate: gap over the head, cm
hud.monster_bar_gap_cm.tip = How far over the monster's head the plate's lower edge hangs; below 0 it lowers into the head. The head's height is worked out from the game's own anchor of the plate and the monster's place. Live.
hud.monster_height.label = Name over a monster: height, %
hud.monster_height.tip = First person (F4) only, while the plate over the monster's head (above) is off. The name and health bar over the monster you target, higher (+) or lower (-): % of the screen's height; the whole plate moves, still following its monster. Too high, or cut off at the top of your view? Lower it (try -15 to -30). 0 = where the game puts it. Monsters and NPCs; the plate that hangs over the monster (the game's controller layout, the one D2R VR plays in). Live. Needs no ReShade effect.
hud.monster_depth_body.label = Name over a monster: at its monster, %
hud.monster_depth_body.tip = First person (F4) in stereo. The game draws the plate in both eyes on the same spot, so in the headset it floats far off, not on its monster. Here it is set at its monster's depth, by the monster's distance from you, as the item labels are (Item labels: at their items): 100 = exactly there, 0 = where the game leaves it (the stereo depth below). Live.
hud.monster_near_body.label = Name over a monster: stereo depth
hud.monster_near_body.tip = First person (F4) in stereo: the name and bar over the monster you target nearer (+) or farther (-), % of the half screen - its own, apart from the item labels' ("Item labels: stereo depth on top" above does not move it). Live.

# --- Low life: red heartbeat vignette ---
group.low_life_red_heartbeat_vignette = Low life: red heartbeat vignette
group.low_life_red_heartbeat_vignette.help = A warning when your life is low (native OpenXR, F4): the edges of your view tint red and beat like a heart, with a heartbeat in the controllers if you like. The sliders set when it starts, how red, how large and its shape. A wounded mercenary can be tinted red too. Needs the new D2R_DepthFog.fx.
hud.low_hp_vignette.label = Red heartbeat vignette at low life
hud.low_hp_vignette.tip = Native OpenXR, first person (F4). While your life is under the threshold below, the edges of what you see tint deep red and beat like a heart - a double beat, then a rest - faster and redder the lower your life goes. It comes up within a second of dropping under the threshold, goes out after you heal a little above it, and is never there when you are dead, in a menu or outside a game. It is a colour over the picture's edges only: the picture is not scaled, moved or shaken. The sliders below set how it looks. Needs the new D2R_DepthFog.fx in ReShade, copied in with the DLL. Off: the picture exactly as before. Live.
hud.low_hp_threshold.label = Low life: from, % of your life
hud.low_hp_threshold.tip = The vignette comes on when your life falls under this share of its maximum and goes out a little above it. Live.
hud.low_hp_intensity_start.label = Intensity just under the threshold
hud.low_hp_intensity_start.tip = How red the edges are at the top of a beat when your life has only just fallen under the threshold (1 = solid red at the rim). Between this and the next slider the intensity follows your life in a straight line - and so does the heartbeat in the controllers. Live.
hud.low_hp_intensity_end.label = Intensity at the lowest life
hud.low_hp_intensity_end.tip = How red the edges are at the top of a beat when you are nearly dead. Live.
hud.low_hp_saturation.label = Red: saturation
hud.low_hp_saturation.tip = The colour of the vignette: 0 = a dark grey, one that only darkens the edges; 1 = the full deep red. Live.
hud.low_hp_radius.label = Vignette size, % of the view
hud.low_hp_radius.tip = How far in from the edge of the view the colour reaches, in % of the view's ANGLE: small = only a thin rim, large = a deep vignette. 100 minus this is the clear middle: at 40 the middle 60% stays clear (on a 100 degree view that is the middle 60 degrees). The plugin takes your headset's real field of view from its runtime, so the same value is the same angle on any headset; headsets differ in what you see through the lenses, so set it to your taste. 40 is about what the first version did. Live.
hud.low_hp_softness.label = Edge: softness
hud.low_hp_softness.tip = How gradually the colour builds up over that reach: 1 = a smooth fade all the way in, 0 = a short ramp and then flat colour to the rim. Live.
hud.low_hp_roundness.label = Shape: oval .. rounded square
hud.low_hp_roundness.tip = The shape of the clear middle: 2 = an oval, higher = a rounder and rounder rectangle (the clear middle then reaches further toward the corners of the view). Live.
hud.low_hp_gentle.label = Gentle (slower, softer)
hud.low_hp_gentle.tip = A slower heartbeat (50 up to 72 beats a minute, against 60 up to 90), a softer beat with a shallower pulse, less red and a slower fade - for anyone who finds the pulse in the corner of the eye too much. Live.
hud.low_hp_haptics.label = Heartbeat in the controllers
hud.low_hp_haptics.tip = A short pulse in both controllers on each beat, as the red climbs, stronger the lower your life is (the same line as the intensity above). Needs Controller vibration (Stereo > Native OpenXR) ticked; its own strength slider applies too. Live.
hud.low_hp_haptics_strength.label = Heartbeat in the controllers: strength
hud.low_hp_haptics_strength.tip = A scale on the pulse's strength: 1 = about half the motor's strength at the lowest life, and weaker the higher your life. The pulse is never stronger than four fifths of the motor, so 2 is plenty. Live.
hud.merc_tint.label = Wounded mercenary tinted red (F4)
hud.merc_tint.tip = VR first person (F4). While your mercenary is under the threshold below of its life, the effect tints its body red, so you see when it needs a potion. Drawn by the plugin over the finished picture: the merc is found and its life only READ, nothing in the game is changed (no state set on the merc, unlike d2r-pcvr's version of the idea). Needs the new D2R_DepthFog.fx in ReShade, copied in with the DLL. Idea: bearstonem/d2r-pcvr. Off: the picture exactly as before. Live.
hud.merc_tint_threshold.label = Mercenary tint: under, % of its life
hud.merc_tint_threshold.tip = The red comes on while the mercenary's life is under this share of its maximum. Live.
hud.merc_tint_strength.label = Mercenary tint: strength
hud.merc_tint_strength.tip = How far the mercenary's colours go toward the red: 1 = fully red. Live.

hud.notice_card.tip = VR first person (F4), native OpenXR. The game's own notice ("Quest log updated", new skill or stat points) sits low in the middle of its interface, where the toolbar's strip is taken out of the picture, so in the headset it was not seen at all. Ticked: that notice - the game's own picture of it, in its language - is cut out and shown on a small card in the room, a metre ahead of where you look when it comes, a little under your eyes, for the seconds below, then it fades. The game's panel itself is left as it is (its timer, its Start button to open the quest log). Idea: bearstonem/d2r-pcvr. Off: as before. Live.

# --- Panels (inventory, trade...) ---
group.panels_inventory_trade = Panels (inventory, trade...)
group.panels_inventory_trade.help = Makes the game's panels (inventory, stash, trader) fit in VR: how far the screen moves away while a panel is open, so all of it is in view, and the game's interface size - VR starts it at 80 % so its edges are not cut off in the headset.
screen.menu_distance_m.label#2 = Screen distance while a panel is open (inventory, trade...), m
screen.menu_distance_m.tip#2 = While the inventory, a trader, the stash or another panel is open in first person (F4), FlatVR moves its screen this far from your eyes, so the whole panel is in view, and brings it back to your own distance when the panel closes - smoothly, in under half a second. Your FlatVR Distance setting is not changed. A screen already farther away than this comes nearer instead. 0 = the screen stays where it is. Needs BodyWalk with the Game Link plugin and FlatVR's "Screen distance follows the game" (on by default). With native OpenXR the flat picture a panel is shown on goes this far, in any view (Stereo > Native OpenXR).
@game.Safe Screen Percent.label = Game interface size, % (restart)
@game.Safe Screen Percent.tip = Below 100 the game lays its whole interface out in a smaller box in the middle of the screen - in every view. At 100, the game's default, the edges of the interface are cut off in the headset (the inventory, the stash and the other panels are wider than the picture; with a trader or the mercenary open beside the inventory the outer columns of both cannot be reached): VR starts it at 80 where you have chosen no other size (the box below; 74 for the headset's own, taller picture) - the most two side panels fit a square picture at. A size of yours other than 100 stays as it is (the line below the box says whether it fits); flat mode keeps your own. Read when the game starts: change it with the game closed, or the game puts its own value back on exit.
hud.safe_screen_vr.label = VR: start the interface at 80 %
hud.safe_screen_vr.tip = On: when the game's interface size is 100 (its default), D2R VR sets 80 for VR - at 100 the edges of the interface are cut off in the headset - when the game starts, or at once with the game closed. The size you had is kept and comes back in flat mode. Any size of yours other than 100 is left alone. Off: the game's interface size is never touched (and an 80 D2R VR set goes back to what you had). With it on a 100 of yours does not stay in VR: untick it to keep 100.

group.toolbar_life_mana_belt_in_first_person = Toolbar (life, mana, belt) in first person
group.toolbar_life_mana_belt_in_first_person.help = Where the game's toolbar (life and mana globes, belt, skill buttons) goes in first person (F4): life and mana as balls on your wrists, the whole toolbar on your chest, low in front, on a forearm, in the picture, or not shown. This one choice sets the two blocks below together.
@toolbar.type.label = Toolbar type (first person, F4)
@toolbar.type.tip = The game's bottom panel is its toolbar: the life and mana globes, the belt and the skill buttons. This one choice sets Hide the game's interface and Where (below) together, so a place always works. Where it is, view by view: F1, F2, F3 and the flat modes - in the picture where the game draws it (those tabs size or move it; set to 'Hung in the room' a view follows this choice like F4). F4: 'Watches' - cut out of the picture, your life and mana as two balls on the wrists (needs D2R_DepthFog.fx in ReShade). 'Chest', 'low in front', 'forearm' - cut out and hung there as the whole toolbar (its size and place are the sliders below). 'In the picture' - left where the game draws it: it moves with your head, at the bottom of your view, in front of your eyes. With a panel open (inventory, stash, trader, the game's menu) the game's whole interface is back in every view, the toolbar with it: in the picture, or at the bottom of the menu panel. Live.
@toolbar.type.choice0 = Watches on the wrists: life and mana
@toolbar.type.choice1 = Whole toolbar on the chest, low
@toolbar.type.choice2 = Whole toolbar low in front of you
@toolbar.type.choice3 = Whole toolbar on the left forearm
@toolbar.type.choice4 = Whole toolbar on the right forearm
@toolbar.type.choice5 = Not shown
@toolbar.type.choice6 = In the picture, in front of your eyes

Another click - on the big map or pointing away - puts the map back in your hand. While the laser points at the map the trigger is the laser's, not an attack. Unticked: no laser on the map. Live.

hud.map_big_follow.label = Big map in front: stays in the room, follows slowly

A square 2048 picture at Safe Screen Percent 80 wants about 3 - 4. Live; tick "Show the cut strip" below to see where its top edge is.
hud.hide_down_pct.label = Toolbar cut: lower, % of the picture

hud.hand_vitals_orb_fill.label = Fill direction
